anti_patterns: Restaking into AVSs with subjective slashing conditions: slash only for on-chain-checkable, objectively attributable faults; subjective conditions defeat risk modeling
Single-operator concentration: delegating ecosystem-wide stake to one operator recreates the centralization restaking was meant to dissolve
Blind delegation: delegating without auditing each AVS operator set, quorum rules, and allocation delays
Ignoring correlated-slashing leverage: treating restaked yield as free without modeling slashable stake summed across all opted-in AVSs
Skipping withdrawal-delay planning: assuming restaked ETH is liquid when undelegation plus beacon exit queues impose multi-day to multi-week delays
Running AVS operator software without liveness monitoring: downtime in data-availability or keeper AVSs triggers penalties that L1 validation alone never incurred
avoid_when: Staker cannot audit or continuously monitor each AVS slashing contract and operator allocation
Liquidity is required at short notice: beacon exit queues plus EigenLayer withdrawal delays block fast exits
Only one protocol needs securing: direct validation or a dedicated operator set is simpler than pooled security
Slashing conditions are subjective or governance-controlled rather than objectively attributable on-chain
Operational maturity is low: running beacon validators plus AVS operator software exceeds team capacity
Regulatory posture forbids reuse of staked collateral across multiple protocols
benefits: Cold-start security solved: new AVSs rent cryptoeconomic security from existing ETH stake instead of bootstrapping a validator set
Capital efficiency: one unit of staked ETH secures Ethereum plus N opted-in AVSs simultaneously
Additional yield: restakers earn AVS fees and rewards on top of beacon-chain issuance without extra collateral
Programmable quorums: AVSs define operator sets, supported strategies, and minimum-stake thresholds per quorum
Opt-in risk isolation: stakers choose operators whose AVS portfolio matches their risk tolerance and can redelegate
Objective slashing: penalties trigger only on provable, on-chain-checkable faults, keeping risk modelable
best_practices: Delegate only to operators whose AVS portfolio you have audited: read each operator set, quorum config, and slashing contract
Monitor operator allocations continuously: previously delegated stake becomes slashable when the operator joins new operator sets
Prefer AVSs with objectively attributable slashing (double-signing, failed proof-of-custody) over subjective or governance slashing
Complete EigenPod checkpoints regularly so consensus and execution-layer yield is accounted as shares
Plan exits around both delays: EigenLayer withdrawal delay plus beacon-chain exit queue before assuming liquidity
Run AVS operator software with liveness alerting equal to beacon-validator monitoring; keep a redelegation target ready
component_types: EigenPod: per-staker proxy contract holding beacon withdrawal credentials and proving balances via EIP-4788 beacon proofs
EigenPodManager: deploys EigenPods, verifies withdrawal credentials, mints beacon-ETH strategy shares
DelegationManager: tracks staker-to-operator delegation, queues withdrawals, enforces withdrawal delay
AllocationManager: operator-set registry where operators allocate slashable stake proportions per AVS
Operator: runs beacon validator plus AVS software; receives delegation and earns commissions
AVS Contracts: operator-set coordinators, stake registries, BLS aggregate-key registries, and dispute-resolution slashers
Slasher / Dispute Resolution: freezes operators on proven faults and burns or redistributes slashable shares
Beacon Chain Oracle (EIP-4788): supplies beacon block roots so EigenPods verify validators trustlessly
context: Ethereum validators lock ETH to secure layer 1, leaving tens of billions in staked capital idle while new protocols (data-availability layers, bridges, oracles, sequencers, keeper networks, called actively validated services or AVSs) face a cold-start problem: bootstrapping their own validator set is expensive and insecure. Native restaking lets a validator point its beacon-chain withdrawal credentials at its EigenPod, prove the credentials on-chain, receive restaked shares, and delegate them to an operator that opts into securing chosen AVSs. The same ETH then underwrites Ethereum consensus plus each opted-in AVS, earning stacked rewards in exchange for stacked, additive slashing conditions.
design_principles: Reuse, Don't Rebuild Security: extend Ethereum cryptoeconomic trust to new services instead of bootstrapping parallel validator sets
Opt-In Accountability: no stake becomes slashable by an AVS without explicit operator registration and allocation
Objective Faults Only: slash exclusively for provable, on-chain-checkable misbehavior so risk stays modelable
Additive Risk Disclosure: every opted-in operator set adds slashable exposure; total risk is the sum, never the maximum
Exitability: delegation changes and withdrawals must always be possible through bounded-delay queues
Minimal Trust in Middleware: AVS contracts are per-service and untrusted; only the core EigenLayer contracts anchor security
name: native-restaking-eigenlayer
tradeoffs: Correlated slashing leverage: one ETH backs N AVSs, so a single operator fault can burn collateral shared across services
Liveness burden: operators must run beacon validation plus every opted-in AVS stack correctly or face penalties
Illiquidity: natively restaked ETH stays locked behind beacon exit queues plus a 7-day EigenLayer withdrawal delay
No composability: unlike liquid staking or liquid restaking tokens, beacon-locked position cannot be used in DeFi
Contract and operator trust: EigenLayer core plus each AVS slashing contract and operator become trusted parties
Governance complexity: stakers must continuously audit operator AVS portfolios, quorum changes, and allocation updates
use_cases: Data-availability layer (EigenDA) secured by restaked ETH instead of a new token validator set
Decentralized sequencer or prover network renting Ethereum-level economic security
Cross-chain bridge or oracle network using restaked quorums for attestation
Keeper and automation networks paying restakers for liveness-critical task execution
Middleware services needing BLS-aggregated operator signatures with slashable commitments
